12-01-w1: The whole amount fills all eight boxes. That is why we divide by 3 + 5, not by 3 or 5 alone.
The first person gets three identical €10 boxes. Keep the full calculation visible so you can see where the €10 came from.
The other person gets five of the same boxes. The two shares use all eight boxes without changing their size.
12-01-w2: Here the amount given belongs to one group, not the whole. Seven blue parts contain 28 counters, so each part contains four.
The ratio gives four red parts. Each has the same size as a blue part.
The question also asks for the whole collection. Add both colours, not the two ratio numbers.
12-01-w3: The 1.4 litres is only the concentrate, so it fills 2 parts, not all 7. Find one part from it, then give water 5 of those parts.
The concentrate stays at 1.4 litres. In the new 1:4 ratio, the water must be four times that amount.
The question asks what to ADD, not the final amount of water. Remove the 3.5 litres already present from the 5.6 litres needed.
12-01-w4: The top counts unfinished work: all the worker-days minus those already done. The bottom counts the four workers left to do it.
There are 60 worker-days of work left. Four workers do 4 worker-days each day, so they need 60 ÷ 4 = 15 more days.
These 15 days start after the first five. Add them only when finding the total duration.
12-03-w1: Average speed asks how far you travel per hour. Share the total distance equally across the three hours.
12-03-w2: The speed is per HOUR, so express the time in hours too. Twenty-five minutes is 25/60 of an hour; travel that fraction of 72 kilometres.
12-03-w3: Find time from distance ÷ speed for each section. The two times belong to the same journey, so add them.
Now use the whole trip: all five kilometres divided by the whole half-hour. Do not average the speeds unless the times are equal.
12-03-w4: Moving time counts only the outward and return journeys. Each time is its distance divided by its speed.
Overall time includes the half-hour rest. The distance stays 120 km, but the larger time makes the overall average speed smaller.
20-02-w1: Every notebook adds the same €3. With no starting charge, multiply the number of notebooks by three.
Put seven into the quantity slot. The rule stays the same; only the input changes.
20-02-w2: Divide each y by its matching x. The same result each time means every 1 of x is worth 3.5 of y.
Use that same value for 10 units. This works because the table shows direct proportion.
20-02-w3: Split the bill into a fixed €5 and a distance part. Only the distance part grows when you travel farther.
Compare a journey with double the distance. Keep the fixed fee once in each bill.
Twice €11 would be €22, but the second bill is €17. A straight line with a starting fee is not direct proportion.
20-02-w4: At the meeting point both rules give the same cost, so set them equal using the same n.
Take 2.5n from both sides, then divide by 1.5. Put n = 8 into either rule to find the cost.
To find when B wins, make its full cost less than A’s. Rearrange the inequality just as you did the equation.
The question needs whole numbers, so start at the next whole number above eight. Only A has no starting fee.
11-01-w1: A midpoint is halfway along in both directions. That is why you average the x-values and the y-values separately.
5 is halfway between 2 and 8, and 7 is halfway between 4 and 10. Write the answer as a point, in brackets.
11-01-w2: Subtracting the coordinates gives the two short sides of a right-angled triangle. Keep the bracket around −1 so that the subtraction becomes 5 + 1.
The direct distance is the longest side, so Pythagoras applies. Square first, then add, then take the square root.
11-01-w3: This is the midpoint formula run backwards. You know the average and one of the two numbers, so write an equation for each coordinate.
Multiply both sides by 2 to undo the halving. Now each equation says what the two coordinates add up to.
Take A’s coordinate away from each total to get B’s. Watch the sign when you take 4 away from −4.
11-01-w4: Each sloping side is the long side of a right-angled triangle, 6 across and 8 up or down. Squaring removes any minus sign, so both lengths come to 10.
A and C have the same y, so AC is flat and its length is just the difference in x. The perimeter adds all three sides.
A median joins a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side. So you need the midpoint of AC first.
M has the same x as B, so BM is a vertical line. Its length is just the difference in y.
11-02-w1: Start from the same point on top and underneath. The line climbs 8 while it goes 4 across, so it climbs 2 for every 1 across.
11-02-w2: Subtracting −3 underneath becomes adding 3. The top is negative because y falls, so the slope is negative.
11-02-w3: Both points have y = 3, so the line is flat. Zero divided by 5 is 0, and 0 is a perfectly good slope.
Both points have x = 4, so the line goes straight up. You would have to divide by 0, which has no answer, so the slope is undefined.
11-02-w4: Three points are in one line only if the steepness never changes. So compare the slope from A to B with the slope from B to C.
The same slope and a shared point B mean one straight line runs through all three.
From C, x goes up by 2. With slope −2, y drops by 2 for each 1 across, so it drops by 4.
11-03-w1: The point has x = 0, so it sits on the y-axis. That means you already know c, and y = mx + c is the quickest form.
Put the slope in front of x and the intercept at the end. Keep the minus sign of −2.
11-03-w2: This point is not on the y-axis, so you do not know c yet. The point-slope formula works from any point.
The −2 multiplies both terms in the bracket. A minus times a minus gives +8.
Add 1 to both sides to leave y on its own. Now the slope and the intercept are easy to read.
11-03-w3: Two points give you a slope. You need it before you can write any equation of the line.
Use either point with the slope. Here x − (−2) becomes x + 2.
Multiply both sides by 2 to clear the fraction. The final form needs whole numbers.
Move every term to one side so the other side is 0. Keeping x positive gives the tidy form.
11-03-w4: The given line has slope 2. A line at right angles to it has the flipped fraction with the opposite sign.
The point has y = −1, so y − (−1) becomes y + 1. Writing the slope as a division by 2 keeps the next move simple.
Multiply both sides by 2 to clear the fraction. The minus sign applies to both x and −3, giving −x + 3.
Bring every term to the left so that the right side is 0.
Every point on the x-axis has y = 0. Putting y = 0 into the equation leaves only x to find.
11-04-w1: The equation already starts with y =, so just read it. The number in front of x is the slope. The number on its own, with its sign, is c.
11-04-w2: You can read the slope only when y is on its own. Start from the equation as given.
Take 3x from both sides so that the y term is alone on the left.
Divide every term by 2, not just the first one. Now the number in front of x is the slope.
11-04-w3: The y-intercept gives c = 6 straight away. The point must fit the equation, so putting its x and y in makes an equation with only m.
Take 6 from both sides, then divide by 4. This is an ordinary equation with one unknown.
Put the slope you found back into y = mx + 6 to finish the equation.
11-04-w4: A flat line does not rise, so the number in front of x must be 0. That number is k − 2.
A line through (0, 0) has y = 0 when x = 0. So the number on its own, 3k, must be 0.
11-05-w1: Parallel lines have the same slope. These are two different lines because they cross the y-axis at different heights, 1 and −5.
11-05-w2: Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1. Flipping 3/4 and changing the sign is the quick way to make that happen.
11-05-w3: A parallel line has the same slope. Getting y on its own in 2x + 3y = 6 shows that the slope is −2/3.
Use the point-slope formula with the point (3, 4). Writing the 3 underneath keeps the fraction in one place.
Multiply both sides by 3 to clear the fraction. −2 times −3 gives +6.
Add 2x and 12 to both sides. The left side now matches the original line, which shows the slope is the same.
11-05-w4: A right angle shows up as two sides whose slopes multiply to −1. So find the slopes of the sides first.
AB and BC meet at B, and their slopes multiply to −1. So the right angle is at B.
Comparing squared lengths avoids square roots. If two of them were equal, the triangle would be isosceles.
20, 5 and 25 are all different, so no two sides are equal. Scalene means all three sides have different lengths.
11-06-w1: Any x-value works, so choose easy ones. x = 0 is the easiest and gives the point on the y-axis.
A second point is enough to fix a straight line. Choose it a little away from the first so the line is easier to draw accurately.
11-06-w2: The line crosses the x-axis where y is 0. Putting y = 0 in leaves an equation with only x.
The line crosses the y-axis where x is 0. Putting x = 0 in leaves only y.
Two points fix one straight line. Use a ruler and carry the line on past both points.
11-06-w3: The crossing point must obey both equations at once. One fixes x and the other fixes y, so there is nothing to solve.
The form y = mx + c needs a slope m. A vertical line has run zero, so it has no slope value to use.
11-06-w4: A point is on the line only if it makes the equation true. The second point gives −12, so it is not on the line.
Dividing 12 by −2 gives −6. The student lost the minus sign.
A third point guards against a slip. If all three points line up on the page, the drawing is right.
11-07-w1: The crossing point lies on both lines, so its x and y must fit both equations.
Both lines have the same y at the crossing. The second line says that y is 6, so 2x must equal 6.
Divide by 2 to find x. An intersection is a point, so give both coordinates.
11-07-w2: The crossing point fits both equations at once. Write them side by side.
Both right-hand sides equal the same y, so they equal each other. That leaves one equation with only x.
Take x from both sides and add 2 to both sides. Each move keeps the two sides balanced.
Divide by 2 to find x, then put x into the simpler equation to find y. Finish with a coordinate pair.
11-07-w3: Neither equation starts with y =, so look for another way in. One has +y and the other has −y.
Adding the equations makes +y and −y cancel. That leaves only x to solve.
Divide by 3 to find x. Then put x = 3 into an original equation to bring y back.
Take 6 from both sides to find y. Write the answer as a point.
11-07-w4: You need the first line’s equation before you can find a crossing. The point (0, 6) gives c = 6, and the slope is −6/4 = −1.5.
At the crossing both lines have the same y, so set the two expressions equal.
Add 1.5x to both sides and take 1 from both sides. This gathers the x terms on one side.
Divide 5 by 2.5 to find x. Then y = x + 1 gives the height of the crossing.
A line goes on for ever, but a segment stops at its endpoints. x = 2 is between 0 and 4, so the point is on the segment.
11-08-w1: Slope is the change up divided by the change across. Up is kilometres and across is hours, so the slope is a speed in km/h.
11-08-w2: Take final minus starting value for both volume and time. The volume change is negative because the tank is losing water.
Put the slope into words with its units. The sign gives the direction: down by 9 litres every minute.
11-08-w3: The number multiplied by d is charged for every kilometre. The number on its own is charged once, however far you go.
Put 7 in place of d. Multiply before you add, so that the fixed €4 is added only once.
11-08-w4: One kilometre is 1000 metres, so the drop per kilometre is 1000 times the drop per metre. Both models describe the same cooling.
This model wants the height in metres, so use 1500.
This model wants kilometres, so use 1.5. Getting 9°C again shows that the two models agree.
20-01-w1: The steepness of the line is the speed. Thirty minutes is half an hour, so dividing by 0.5 gives kilometres per hour.
20-01-w2: The graph is flat between 20 and 30 minutes. A flat part means the distance from home is not changing.
The traveller goes 2 km out, then 2 km back. The graph ends at 0, but both parts were travelled.
20-01-w3: Average speed is total distance over total time. Here the time includes the 10 minute rest, and the minutes are turned into hours.
For the moving speed, leave the rest out of the time. The distance is still 4 km, so the answer is larger.
20-01-w4: They meet when they are at the same place at the same time. So make the two position rules equal.
Add 2t to both sides and take 2 from both sides. Then divide by 6.
Put t = 2 into A’s rule to find the place. B’s rule gives the same answer, which confirms it.
20-03-w1: A flat graph means the quantity on the vertical axis is not changing. Here that quantity is the height of the water.
The same height in a fixed tank means the same volume. That does not prove the tap is off: water could enter and leave at equal rates.
20-03-w2: Every layer of the tank is the same size, so each minute’s water raises the level by the same amount. Equal rises in equal times make a straight line.
20-03-w3: The water arrives at the same rate, but a wide layer takes more water to fill. So the level climbs more slowly and the graph gets flatter.
20-03-w4: Height rises at flow divided by area. In the lower section that is 5 cm each minute, and it lasts until the 10 cm mark at 2 minutes.
After 2 minutes the level starts from 10 cm and climbs more slowly, because the area is bigger. Count only the time since the 2 minute mark.
01-01-w1: Spot two kinds of term: x terms and plain numbers. The minus sign belongs to the 5x.
Put like terms side by side. Each term keeps its own sign when it moves.
Eight x take away five x leaves three x. An x term and a plain number are different kinds, so they cannot be joined.
01-01-w2: There are three kinds here: a terms, b terms and a plain number. Different letters never combine.
Move matching letters together. The 2b keeps its minus sign.
Count each kind on its own. Seven b take away two b leaves five b. The last number has no partner.
01-01-w3: Look for three kinds: x² terms, x terms and plain numbers. The lone −x² is one x² taken away.
Group by power, highest first. Every term carries the sign in front of it.
Work through one group at a time. Seven take away twelve goes below zero, so the number part is negative.
01-01-w4: The two sides must be equal for every value of x, not just one. That is a strong condition.
Collect the x terms and the plain numbers on the left. Now both sides have the same shape.
If two expressions agree for every x, the numbers in front of x must match. The plain numbers must match too.
Each small equation has one unknown. Undo the subtraction in one and the addition in the other.
01-02-w1: Two terms times two terms means four products. A grid gives each one a box.
The x multiplies both terms of the second bracket. Then the 2 multiplies both. That makes four products.
Only the two x terms are the same kind. The x² term and the plain number stay as they are.
01-02-w2: Read the first bracket as 3x and −2. The minus sign travels with the 2.
The −2 row gives two negative products, because a negative times a positive is negative.
Only the two x terms combine. The other two terms have no partners.
01-02-w3: Both brackets hold a negative term. Keep each minus sign with its number.
Two products are negative. The last one is a negative times a negative, which is positive.
Both x terms are negative, so together they make a bigger negative.
01-02-w4: Area of a rectangle is length times width. Each side is a bracket here, so multiply the brackets.
Four products again. The −2 makes two of them negative.
The two x terms are like terms. Together they leave one x taken away, written −x.
Now x has a value, so replace every x with 5. Square before you multiply by 2.
01-03-w1: Two terms times three terms means six products. Use a grid with two rows and three columns.
The first three products come from x, the last three from 2. Multiplying by x raises each power by one.
Match the powers: two x² terms and two x terms. The x³ term and the plain number stand alone.
01-03-w2: The first bracket is x and −3. The −3 must multiply all three terms of the second bracket.
Multiplying by −3 flips every sign in that row. A negative times a negative gives the positive number at the end.
Collect each power separately. Two x² take away three x² leaves one x² taken away.
01-03-w3: Plan two rows: one for 2x and one for −1. Each row has three products.
In the 2x row, multiply the numbers and raise each power by one. The −1 row just changes every sign.
Collect matching powers. The two x² terms are both negative, so they make a bigger negative.
01-03-w4: Volume of a box is length times width times height. Multiply three things, two at a time.
Do the two brackets first. That leaves one term outside one bracket, which is easier.
The x outside multiplies every term inside. Each power goes up by one.
Put 2 in for every x. Work out the powers first, then multiply, then add.
01-04-w1: Brackets go around −2 each time it replaces x. They keep the minus sign with the 2.
Powers come first, and a negative squared is positive. Taking away a negative product is the same as adding.
Both parts are positive, so the answer is positive. A negative answer here would point to a sign slip.
01-04-w2: Every a becomes (−1) and every b becomes 3. Do not calculate yet, just replace.
Take one term at a time. The middle term multiplies two negatives, so it turns positive.
All three parts are positive, so simply add them.
01-04-w3: Replace x and y on the top and on the bottom. Brackets keep the negative quarter together.
Taking away a negative quarter adds a quarter. Adding a negative quarter takes a quarter away.
Write each line in quarters so that the top and the bottom are single fractions.
How many quarters fit into five quarters? Dividing by a quarter is the same as multiplying by 4.
01-04-w4: With no brackets, the power is done first. Only a is squared, and the minus is put on afterwards.
Here the bracket comes first. The opposite of −2 is 2, and then 2 is squared.
The two values are opposites, so they cancel. The brackets made the only difference.
01-05-w1: x was multiplied by 5, then 7 was added. To get back to x, undo these in reverse order.
Take 7 from both sides. The scale stays balanced and the added 7 is gone.
Five lots of x make 25, so share both sides into five equal parts.
01-05-w2: x appears on both sides. The aim is to gather the x terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
The 4 multiplies both terms in the bracket, the x and the −2.
Take 2x from both sides. Now x appears on the left only.
Add 8 to both sides to undo the subtraction of 8.
Two lots of x make 18. Halve both sides to find one x.
01-05-w3: There are two brackets to multiply out. Treat the second multiplier as −2, not 2.
The −2 multiplies both x and 1, so both come out negative. This is where most slips happen.
Collect the x terms, then the numbers. Two negative numbers together make a bigger negative.
Add 17 to both sides to undo the subtraction of 17.
Four lots of x make 28, so divide both sides by 4.
01-05-w4: Fractions make this look hard. Clear them first by multiplying by a number that 3 and 4 both divide into.
Every term is multiplied by 12, including the 2 on the right. Brackets keep each top line together.
The −3 multiplies both x and 2. Forgetting the second one is the usual mistake.
Collect the x terms and the numbers on the left. Now it is an ordinary two-step equation.
Add 10 to both sides to undo the subtraction of 10.
34 does not divide evenly by 5. A fraction answer is fine, so leave it exact.
01-06-w1: Give the unknown number a name. Then follow the words in order: five times it, then minus 3.
Add 3 to both sides to undo the subtraction of 3.
Five lots of the number make 30, so divide both sides by 5.
01-06-w2: Consecutive integers are one apart. If the smaller is n, the next is n + 1, so one letter covers both.
Collect the two n terms. Now it is a two-step equation.
Halve both sides to find the smaller integer.
The question asks for both numbers. The second is one more than the first.
01-06-w3: One letter is enough. The length is described using the width, so the width and the length both use w.
Multiply out the bracket, then collect the w terms.
Four lots of the width make 36, so divide both sides by 4.
The width is not the final answer. Find the length, then multiply to get the area in square centimetres.
01-06-w4: In 6 years both ages go up by 6. The parent's new age equals 2.5 times the child's new age.
The 2.5 multiplies both terms in the bracket, the x and the 6.
Take 2.5x from both sides and take 6 from both sides. The x terms end up on the left, the numbers on the right.
Divide both sides by 1.5. Nine holds six lots of 1.5.
x is the child's age. The parent is four times that, so give both ages.
01-07-w1: Dividing asks what multiplies x + 3 to make the top line. The bottom cannot be zero, so x cannot be −3.
The missing bracket must start with x. Its number must give 15 when multiplied by 3.
The same bracket multiplies the top and the bottom, so it cancels. A bracket cancels only as a whole, never one term from inside it.
01-07-w2: Find the answer one term at a time, starting with the highest power.
x times 2x gives the 2x² you need. That product also uses up 8x, one more than you have, so one x must be taken away.
The first part divides exactly. What is left still has to be divided.
What is left is exactly −1 lot of the divisor. So the last term is −1 and nothing remains.
01-07-w3: An x³ expression divided by a bracket with x gives an x² expression. Expect three terms in the answer: an x² term, an x term and a number.
x times x² makes the x³ you need. Taking away x² lots of the divisor leaves a shorter top line.
Now match the −x² at the front, so the next term is −x. Watch the signs when you take the product away.
What is left is exactly −6 lots of the divisor. Nothing remains, so the division is exact.
01-07-w4: Work from the highest power down. Each term of the answer removes the first term of what is left.
x times 2x² makes the 2x³ you need. That also uses 4x², one more than you have, so one x² is left to take away.
The next term is −x. Take away the whole product, both of its terms.
What is left is exactly −6 lots of the divisor. Nothing remains.
An exact division means the cubic equals the divisor times the answer. That product is the factorised form asked for.
01-08-w1: Write every number as a decimal so they are easy to compare. Further left on the number line means smaller, so −3 comes before −1.5.
01-08-w2: A number is rational if you can write it as one whole number over another. Any integer can be written over 1.
2 is not a square number (1, 4, 9 and so on), so its square root never ends or repeats as a decimal. An integer has no fraction part.
01-08-w3: Any fraction between 2 and 3 will do. Halfway is the easiest one to find.
Square the two ends to get 4 and 9. A whole number between them that is not a square number has an irrational square root.
01-08-w4: One example that breaks the rule is enough to answer no. Opposite numbers cancel to zero.
Here the irrational parts add up instead of cancelling, so the sum stays irrational.
01-09-w1: Solve it like an equation. The only difference is the sign in the middle.
Taking 4 from both sides does not change which side is smaller, so the sign stays.
5 itself is not allowed, so the circle is open. Smaller numbers are to the left.
01-09-w2: The sign here means greater than or equal to. Solve it the way you would solve an equation.
Adding 2 to both sides never changes the direction of the sign.
You divide by positive 3, so the sign stays the same. Only a negative divisor turns it.
4 is allowed because of the or equal to part, so the circle is filled. Bigger numbers are to the right.
01-09-w3: The x term is −2x. Its minus sign matters later, so keep it attached.
Subtracting 7 from both sides does not turn the sign. Subtracting never does.
Now you divide by a negative number, so the sign turns around. Test x = −5: the left side is 17, which is greater than 15.
01-09-w4: The fare is the €4 start plus €2.50 for every kilometre. At most €22 means the fare can equal €22 or be less.
Take the €4 start charge from both sides. What is left pays for distance.
You divide by positive 2.5, so the sign stays the same.
A distance cannot be negative, so d starts at 0. For whole kilometres round down, because 8 kilometres would cost €24.
02-01-w1: Look at the numbers first. Both 12 and 18 are in the 6 times table, and 6 is the biggest number that divides both.
Each term is divided by 6, and what is left goes inside the bracket. Multiplying back should return 12x + 18.
02-01-w2: Check numbers and letters separately. 5 divides both 15 and 10, and each term has at least one letter a.
Taking out 5a leaves 3a from the first term and 2 from the second. The minus sign between them stays.
02-01-w3: There are three terms, so the factor must divide all three. The smallest number is 6, and it divides 18 and 24 as well.
The last term is exactly 6xy, so dividing it leaves 1. Leaving that place empty would lose a term when you multiply back.
02-01-w4: The first term is negative. The question wants a positive first term inside the bracket, so the factor you take out must be negative.
Dividing by a negative changes each sign. The first term becomes +2x and the second becomes −3.
Square −2 first to get +4. The bracket is −7, and a negative times a negative gives a positive answer.
02-02-w1: No single factor divides all four terms. Pairs are the next thing to try: the first two share the letter a and the last two share the letter b.
Both pairs leave the same bracket, x + y. Matching brackets tell you the grouping has worked.
The bracket is multiplied by a and then by b. Altogether it is multiplied by (a + b), just as 2k + 3k is 5k.
02-02-w2: The four terms come in two natural pairs. The first pair shares 3x and the second pair shares 2.
Both brackets are x + 2. If they did not match, you would try a different factor or a different pairing.
The repeated bracket comes out as one factor. What was in front of it, 3x and 2, forms the other bracket.
02-02-w3: The third term is negative. That is a signal to take a negative number out of the second pair.
Taking out −3 turns +12 into −4 inside the bracket, because −3 × −4 = +12. Now both brackets read y − 4.
The shared bracket y − 4 comes out. The parts left in front, x and −3, make the other bracket.
02-02-w4: There are four terms and no factor shared by all of them. Pair the first two and the last two.
The first pair shares x². Taking −9 out of the second pair makes its bracket x − 2 as well.
The bracket x − 2 comes out, leaving x² − 9. Do not stop yet: check each bracket for another pattern.
x² − 9 is a square minus a square, so it splits again. Factorising fully means no bracket can be factorised further.
02-03-w1: There are two terms with a minus between them. Check whether each one is a square.
Writing 25 as 5² makes the pattern easy to see: something squared minus something squared.
The two things that were squared, x and 5, go in both brackets. One bracket gets minus and the other gets plus.
02-03-w2: Both numbers, 9 and 16, are squares, and so are a² and b². That is the sign to use this pattern.
The whole of 3a is squared, not just the a. 3a × 3a gives 9a².
3a and 4b go in both brackets, with opposite signs so the middle terms cancel.
02-03-w3: 2 and 50 are not squares, so the pattern does not fit yet. Look for a common factor first.
Taking out 2 leaves x² − 25, which is a square minus a square.
The 2 stays in front for the rest of the question. Only the bracket changes.
02-03-w4: A fourth power is the square of a square: x⁴ = (x²)². And 81 = 9².
Here x² and 9 are the things being squared, so they go in both brackets.
x² − 9 is another square minus a square, so it splits again. x² + 9 has a plus, so it stays as it is.
02-04-w1: The number in front of x² is 1. So you need two numbers that multiply to 20 and add to 9.
4 and 5 fit both conditions. Splitting 9x into 4x + 5x lets you see where the brackets come from.
Each pair has a common factor, and both leave the bracket x + 4.
The shared bracket comes out. The numbers in the two brackets are the 4 and 5 you found.
02-04-w2: The last number is negative, so the two numbers have different signs. They must add to −1.
−4 and +3 multiply to −12 and add to −1. The bigger number takes the minus because the sum is negative.
Both pairs leave x − 4. Taking +3 out of the second pair keeps the −12 correct.
Read the signs straight from your pair: −4 gives (x − 4) and +3 gives (x + 3).
02-04-w3: The product is +20 but the sum is −9. Only two negative numbers can do both.
−4 and −5 multiply to +20 and add to −9.
Take −5 out of the second pair, not +5. That turns +20 into −4 inside the bracket, so the brackets match.
